difficultyReason: The argument turns on a subtle temporal gap: the clinical improvement must be attributable to the drug and not to a concurrent change in patient behavior. The necessary assumption rules out a specific alternative causal pathway, and several distractors are defensible-sounding strengtheners rather than true gap-fillers.
stimulus: Neurologist: Patients in our trial who took the new compound daily for eight weeks showed a statistically significant reduction in migraine frequency. No other pharmacological treatment was administered during this period. We therefore conclude that the compound itself was responsible for the reduction in migraines.
questionStem: The neurologist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The compound has no significant side effects in the patient population studied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patients in the trial did not make lifestyle changes during the eight-week period that could have independently reduced their migraines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The compound would produce the same results in patients outside the trial population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All participants completed the full eight-week course of treatment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Migraine frequency in the trial patients was higher than average before the trial began.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'no other pharmacological treatment' to 'the compound caused the reduction.' But this only holds if non-pharmacological factors — lifestyle changes, stress reduction, dietary shifts — were also absent. Negate B: the patients did make lifestyle changes that could have reduced migraines. The conclusion that the compound caused the reduction collapses entirely.
explanations.A: Side effects are irrelevant to whether the compound caused the reduction in migraines. This is an out-of-scope choice — it concerns safety, not causal attribution.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument rules out other pharmacological treatments but leaves open non-pharmacological explanations. B closes that gap; its negation destroys the causal conclusion.
explanations.C: Generalizability to populations outside the trial is not required for the conclusion, which concerns only the trial patients. This is a scope-shift trap.
explanations.D: Completion rates might affect the strength of the data but are not required for the causal inference; even partial completion would not automatically point to lifestyle changes as the cause.
explanations.E: Baseline migraine frequency relative to population averages has no bearing on whether the compound caused the observed reduction within the trial.

difficultyReason: The argument contains a conditional chain embedded in a policy context. The necessary assumption concerns whether the mechanism the policy relies on was actually operative before the policy change — a chronological subtlety that makes the negation test non-obvious.
stimulus: Economist: Since the city lowered its marginal income tax rate three years ago, annual tax revenues have actually increased. Critics who predicted a revenue shortfall were wrong. This shows that reducing the tax rate caused higher economic activity, which in turn generated more total revenue.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city's population did not increase substantially during the three years following the tax cut.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The critics who predicted a revenue shortfall based their predictions solely on static revenue models.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The increase in tax revenues was not primarily due to factors unrelated to the tax rate reduction, such as national economic growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Other cities that have cut tax rates have also experienced revenue increases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city did not simultaneously reduce its spending on public services during the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes rising revenue to the tax cut via increased economic activity. But if national economic growth — independent of the rate change — drove the increase, the causal chain breaks. Negate C: the revenue increase was primarily due to factors unrelated to the rate reduction. The conclusion that the tax cut caused the increase is unsupported.
explanations.A: Population growth could itself be a confound, but the argument's chain specifically requires ruling out non-rate-related economic factors; population change is a narrower and less central alternative than C.
explanations.B: Whether critics used static models concerns the quality of their predictions, not the causal chain the economist asserts. This is out of scope.
explanations.C: Correct. The economist infers causation from correlation. The argument requires that no external confound explains the revenue increase; C negation destroys the causal conclusion.
explanations.D: Evidence from other cities would strengthen the argument but is not required — the argument concerns only this city. This is a sufficient-not-necessary trap.
explanations.E: Spending levels are not part of the causal mechanism described (tax rate → activity → revenue), so they are irrelevant to the argument's gap.

difficultyReason: The argument uses a linguistic artifact (a word's etymology) to draw a conclusion about ancient cultural practice. The assumption bridges the gap between what the word's form implies and what it must have actually referred to — a subtle evidential link that the negation test exposes only on careful re-reading.
stimulus: Linguist: The Proto-Indo-European root word reconstructed as *welg- is the source of both the Latin word for 'moist' and the Sanskrit word for 'rain.' Both daughter languages preserve the root in contexts exclusively associated with water. We can therefore conclude that speakers of Proto-Indo-European used *welg- to refer to naturally occurring water sources in their environment.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the linguist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Proto-Indo-European speakers lived in a region with plentiful rainfall and surface water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The water-related meanings in the daughter languages were not independently acquired after the languages diverged from Proto-Indo-European.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other Proto-Indo-European root word was also associated with water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linguists can reconstruct Proto-Indo-European vocabulary with complete accuracy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Latin and Sanskrit words derived from *welg- are among the oldest attested words in those languages.

explanations.correct: The argument infers *welg-'s original meaning from its meaning in daughter languages. This works only if those meanings were inherited, not developed independently. Negate B: the water-related meanings were independently acquired after divergence. Then the shared water associations tell us nothing about the proto-language word's meaning, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: The argument concerns the word's meaning, not the ecology of the speakers' homeland. This is an out-of-scope strengthener.
explanations.B: Correct. The entire inference from daughter-language meanings back to proto-language meaning requires that those meanings were inherited, not convergently developed.
explanations.C: The existence of other water-related roots is irrelevant; the argument is about what *welg- meant, not whether it was the only such word. This is a shift-in-scope trap.
explanations.D: 'Complete accuracy' is too strong a requirement — the argument needs only that the reconstruction is reliable enough to support a meaning inference, but more importantly, reconstruction accuracy is not the gap in this argument at all.
explanations.E: The age of attestation in daughter languages has no bearing on whether the shared meanings were inherited versus independently developed.

difficultyReason: The argument draws an ethical conclusion from a legal precedent, requiring an assumption about the relationship between legal and moral obligations. The trap choices are morally resonant but either too strong or subtly reversed in direction.
stimulus: Legal scholar: Courts in this jurisdiction have consistently held that parties to a contract are obligated to disclose information that would be material to the other party's decision to enter the contract. Since the defendant knew that the bridge inspection report was materially relevant to the buyer's decision, the defendant had an obligation to disclose it. The defendant therefore acted wrongly in withholding the report.
questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The buyer would have refused to enter the contract had the report been disclosed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failing to fulfill a legal obligation in this jurisdiction constitutes acting wrongly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The defendant was aware of the court decisions establishing the disclosure obligation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All material information relevant to a contract must always be disclosed regardless of cost.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bridge inspection report accurately reflected the structural condition of the bridge.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'the defendant had a legal obligation to disclose' to 'the defendant acted wrongly.' This requires a bridge between legal obligation and moral wrongness. Negate B: failing to fulfill a legal obligation here does not constitute acting wrongly. The conclusion that the defendant 'acted wrongly' is then unsupported, even if the legal violation is established.
explanations.A: The buyer's counterfactual response would strengthen the argument about harm, but the conclusion is about wrongful action, not about the outcome. The argument does not require the buyer to have behaved differently.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument's conclusion is ethical ('acted wrongly'), but its premises are legal. The bridge between the two domains is precisely what B provides; its negation severs the conclusion from the premises.
explanations.C: Awareness of case law is not required for the obligation to exist or for the action to be wrong — ignorance of the law is not a defense here, and the argument doesn't invoke knowledge of the rule as a premise.
explanations.D: This is too strong — 'regardless of cost' introduces a universal claim the argument does not need. The argument requires only that this disclosure was obligatory, not a universal principle.
explanations.E: The accuracy of the report bears on how harmful the withholding was, not on whether withholding a materially relevant report was legally required and ethically wrong.

difficultyReason: The argument relies on the absence of a species from a fossil record to date the species' extinction. The necessary assumption concerns the completeness of the record for the relevant period — a methodological point that requires careful attention to what the evidence could or could not show.
stimulus: Paleontologist: Fossils of the large marine reptile Xanthosaurus have been recovered from sedimentary deposits dating from 180 to 145 million years ago, but none have been found in deposits laid down after that period. The fossil record for the relevant marine environments is otherwise rich and well-preserved for the subsequent 20 million years. Xanthosaurus therefore became extinct approximately 145 million years ago.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the paleontologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xanthosaurus was the apex predator of its marine environment during its existence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The absence of Xanthosaurus fossils from later deposits is not due to the animal's having migrated to environments that are poorly preserved in the fossil record.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No marine reptile species that appeared after 145 million years ago was closely related to Xanthosaurus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sedimentary deposits containing Xanthosaurus fossils have been thoroughly excavated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Xanthosaurus fossils are as durable as those of other large marine reptiles found in the same deposits.

explanations.correct: The argument infers extinction from absence in the fossil record, and attempts to shore this up by noting that the record is otherwise rich for those later environments. But this only rules out fossilization gaps in environments that were already well-preserved. If Xanthosaurus migrated to a poorly-preserved environment, absence from the well-preserved record proves nothing. Negate B: the absence is due to migration to poorly-preserved environments. The extinction conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Apex predator status is entirely outside the scope of the extinction-dating inference.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument uses the richness of the post-145-million-year record to validate the absence as genuine. But this only works if the animal didn't move to an area where fossilization would be unlikely. Negation destroys the evidential basis for the conclusion.
explanations.C: Phylogenetic relationships to later species are irrelevant to when Xanthosaurus itself went extinct.
explanations.D: Thorough excavation concerns how many fossils we've found in known deposits, but the argument already grants that none have been found after 145 mya — completeness of excavation of the known fossils is not the gap.
explanations.E: Fossil durability affects preservation rates across the same environment, but the argument specifically notes the record is rich; durability differences between species would only matter if we expected to find Xanthosaurus but didn't due to fragility.

difficultyReason: The argument attributes a historical outcome to a specific policy decision, but the necessary assumption is that the policy change was implemented as enacted — a procedural gap that is easy to overlook because readers naturally assume enacted policies are carried out.
stimulus: Historian: In 1847, the colonial administration enacted a policy requiring all grain merchants to register their stores with a central authority. Records show that famines became far less frequent in the region during the two decades following 1847. The registration policy must therefore have contributed to reducing famines by enabling authorities to identify and redistribute grain surpluses.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the historian's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The colonial administration was motivated primarily by humanitarian concerns when enacting the policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grain merchants in the region complied with the registration requirement to a sufficient extent that authorities could track surplus stores.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other administrative reforms were enacted by the colonial government during the same two-decade period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Famines in the region before 1847 were caused exclusively by uneven distribution of grain rather than by crop failures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The colonial administration's records from the period after 1847 accurately reflect the true frequency of famines.

explanations.correct: The causal mechanism the historian proposes is: registration → visibility of surpluses → redistribution → fewer famines. This chain requires that the registration policy was actually used — i.e., that merchants registered to a degree that made tracking possible. Negate B: merchants did not comply sufficiently for authorities to track surpluses. The entire redistributive mechanism breaks down, and the policy cannot have reduced famines in the way described.
explanations.A: The administration's motivations are irrelevant to whether the policy had the stated effect. This is an out-of-scope trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The mechanism requires compliance; without it, the policy is nominal and cannot have enabled redistribution.
explanations.C: Too strong — other concurrent reforms would provide alternative explanations, but the argument doesn't need to be the only explanation, merely a contributing one. Also, the question of other reforms concerns alternative causation rather than a gap in the mechanism described.
explanations.D: 'Exclusively' is too strong; the argument only needs grain redistribution to have been able to reduce famine, not that all past famines were purely distributional.
explanations.E: Record accuracy is a meta-evidential concern and is not a gap within the causal chain the argument constructs.

difficultyReason: The argument moves from a statistical pattern in software adoption to a conclusion about user preference, but the necessary assumption concerns whether the statistical pattern reflects genuine choice rather than constrained options — a subtle distinction that distractors obscure with plausible tech-policy framing.
stimulus: Technology analyst: A survey of enterprise software deployments shows that open-source database systems now account for 58 percent of all new installations, up from 31 percent five years ago. Since enterprises choose software based on their operational needs, this shift demonstrates that open-source databases have become better suited to enterprise operational requirements than proprietary alternatives.
questionStem: The technology analyst's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Open-source databases will continue to gain market share over the next five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The enterprises surveyed represent a cross-section of industries rather than a single sector.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The increased adoption of open-source databases was not driven primarily by cost constraints that made proprietary alternatives unaffordable rather than by operational fit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Open-source database systems have more features than proprietary systems available five years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The enterprises that adopted open-source databases did not later revert to proprietary systems.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that the choice reflects operational suitability because enterprises choose based on operational needs. But if enterprises adopted open-source databases mainly because budget cuts made proprietary software unaffordable, the shift reflects cost constraints, not superior operational fit. Negate C: the increase was driven primarily by cost constraints. The conclusion that open-source systems became better suited to operational requirements is then unsupported.
explanations.A: Future market share trends are outside the scope of an argument about why the past shift occurred. This is a scope-drift trap.
explanations.B: Industry diversity in the survey sample would affect generalizability, but the argument's conclusion is not about all industries — it concerns the demonstrated shift. Survey composition is not the argument's gap.
explanations.C: Correct. The key premise is that enterprises choose based on operational needs; if a non-operational factor (cost) drove the switch, the operational-fit conclusion doesn't follow.
explanations.D: Having more features is a specific way of being better suited operationally, but the argument concludes only that open-source became better suited — not necessarily through feature count. Also, this would make the answer sufficient rather than necessary.
explanations.E: Subsequent reversion would affect long-term conclusions but is not required for the argument's inference about why the shift occurred in the first place.

difficultyReason: The argument draws a conclusion about the intended audience of a Renaissance painting from the physical location of a detail within the composition. The necessary assumption concerns viewing conditions — a subtle perceptual link that most readers take for granted, making the negation test unexpectedly decisive.
stimulus: Art historian: In a 1523 altarpiece, the painter concealed a self-portrait in the lower-left corner of the composition, rendered at a scale requiring close inspection to identify. The altarpiece was installed above the high altar of a private chapel accessible only to the patron's household. The self-portrait was therefore intended to be seen by the patron, not by a general congregation.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the art historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The painter was personally acquainted with the patron before accepting the commission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paintings installed above altars in the sixteenth century were generally intended to be viewed from a distance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The patron's household members regularly approached the altarpiece closely enough to view its details at the scale at which the self-portrait was rendered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The painter did not include any other hidden figures elsewhere in the altarpiece.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The patron commissioned the altarpiece specifically because of the painter's reputation for including self-portraits.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes the self-portrait was intended for the patron based on (1) restricted access — only the household could enter, and (2) small scale — requiring close inspection. But restricted access to a space does not guarantee that viewers approached the work closely. If household members never came near enough to see details at that scale, the self-portrait was effectively invisible to everyone. Negate C: household members did not regularly approach closely enough. The argument that the patron was the intended audience collapses.
explanations.A: Prior acquaintance is not required for the viewing-access argument; the argument depends on physical access to the chapel and the scale of the detail, not on the relationship between artist and patron.
explanations.B: General conventions about altarpiece viewing would undercut the argument rather than support it, and in any case conventions elsewhere have no bearing on what was possible in this specific private chapel.
explanations.C: Correct. The chain requires that restricted access implies the patron could see the detail — but that only holds if those with access actually viewed the work at close range.
explanations.D: Other hidden figures would complicate interpretation of the artist's intent but are not required for the conclusion that this self-portrait was aimed at the patron. This is an out-of-scope trap.
explanations.E: The patron's motivation for the commission has no bearing on whether the viewing conditions existed for the self-portrait to be seen.

difficultyReason: The argument uses a proposed environmental regulation's failure to pass as evidence of legislative priorities, but the necessary assumption concerns whether the vote accurately reflects preferences rather than procedural obstacles — a conditional subtlety that makes most distractors seem relevant.
stimulus: Policy analyst: The legislature recently voted down a bill that would have imposed strict emissions limits on agricultural operations. Since legislators vote in accordance with their constituents' preferences, the defeat of the bill shows that the public in this jurisdiction does not prioritize reducing agricultural emissions over protecting farm revenues.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bill's sponsors did not make procedural errors that caused the bill to fail independent of legislators' views on its merits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Agricultural emissions are a significant contributor to air quality problems in the jurisdiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legislators in this jurisdiction are more responsive to rural constituents than to urban constituents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The public in this jurisdiction is aware of the scientific evidence linking agricultural operations to emissions problems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No similar emissions-limiting legislation will be introduced in the next legislative session.

explanations.correct: The analyst's reasoning is: legislators vote per constituent preferences → bill failed → public prefers farm revenue over emissions control. But this requires the vote to reflect legislative preferences about the bill's merits. If the bill failed due to a procedural technicality (a missed deadline, a quorum failure, a committee error), the vote tells us nothing about legislators' — or constituents' — substantive views. Negate A: the bill did fail due to procedural errors independent of legislators' views. The inference about public priorities collapses.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument requires that the vote outcome tracks legislators' views on the merits, which is only true if non-merit procedural factors didn't determine the outcome.
explanations.B: Whether agricultural emissions are actually significant is an out-of-scope scientific question; the argument concerns what the vote reveals about preferences, not whether the bill addressed a real problem.
explanations.C: Urban vs. rural responsiveness is a plausible concern but not required — the argument only needs that legislators track constituents' preferences generally, not that they do so differentially by geography.
explanations.D: Public awareness of scientific evidence is not a link in the argument's chain; the argument infers preferences from a vote, not from what the public knows.
explanations.E: Future legislative sessions are entirely outside the scope of an argument about what a past vote reveals about current public priorities.

difficultyReason: The argument moves from a philosophical claim about moral desert to a specific normative conclusion about punishment, bridging desert theory with institutional practice. The necessary assumption is a modest defensive claim that is easily confused with two stronger distractor answers that prove too much.
stimulus: Ethicist: Punishment is justified only when the person being punished deserves to suffer for what they have done. A person deserves to suffer only if they acted freely and with full knowledge of the wrongness of their act. Since individuals who commit crimes under severe psychological compulsion do not act freely, they do not deserve punishment.
questionStem: The ethicist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Severe psychological compulsion always completely eliminates an individual's freedom of action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No consideration other than desert could ever justify imposing suffering on an individual who has committed a crime.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Individuals who act under psychological compulsion are not morally responsible for any of their actions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The legal system should not punish individuals who do not deserve punishment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An individual who lacks full knowledge of the wrongness of an act is not acting freely in the relevant sense.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's conclusion is that compelled individuals 'do not deserve punishment,' meaning punishment of them is not justified. The first premise states punishment is justified only when deserved. The argument then establishes that compelled actors don't deserve it. But the conclusion requires that justified punishment is tied exclusively to desert — that no alternative ground (deterrence, incapacitation, public safety) could justify punishing someone who doesn't deserve it. Negate B: some consideration other than desert could justify imposing suffering on a compelled offender. Then the first premise ('only when deserved') would be violated, but more importantly, the argument's conclusion that punishment is not justified would be undermined by that alternative ground.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'always completely eliminates' goes beyond what the argument needs. The argument only requires that severe compulsion eliminates freedom in the specific cases at issue; a universal claim is not required and makes this a sufficient-not-necessary trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument's first premise defines justified punishment as requiring desert. The conclusion that compelled actors don't deserve punishment entails they can't justifiably be punished — but only if desert is the sole ground for justified punishment. Negating B opens an alternative justificatory route and undermines the conclusion.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'any of their actions' introduces a universal that the argument doesn't need. The argument concerns punishment for specific crimes, not global moral responsibility.
explanations.D: This adds an institutional prescription (what the legal system should do) that the argument doesn't assert; the ethicist's conclusion is about justification in principle, not about what legal institutions must do. This is a scope-shift trap.
explanations.E: The argument treats freedom and knowledge as two independent conditions for desert. Whether lack of knowledge affects freedom is an internal conceptual question the argument doesn't require — the premises list them as separate conjuncts.
